#4901. Beyond the Snowflake Myth

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

“Snowflake generation” is a term applied to young people who are quickly overwhelmed or “melted” by commonplace pressures and challenges. The rise in young people’s mental health problems and diagnoses of conditions such as autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are sometimes put in this framework, whereby young people today are less resilient and robust than in previous generations of youth who navigated equally, if not more difficult, environments.

Getting a sound perspective on young people’s well-being is essential to assessing appropriate levels of support: How much do we help them by offering practical, emotional, financial and professional support, and how much does such support hinder their capacity to grow resilience themselves?

Across the past three decades, my views of young people’s challenges and how much support the grown-ups in their lives should offer have changed. At the beginning of this century, I wrote about the split between young people’s realities on the one hand and cultural expectations about maturity on the other. [1] I argued that expecting young people to be adults when they reach the age of legal adulthood was unrealistic and damaging—damaging because parents often felt disappointed or frustrated with what they saw as the delayed development of their children, and young people absorbed this disappointment. I pointed out that the conditions of young people today are thin on intergenerational social capital—a deep sense of belonging and a community on which they can draw for informal, personal support. Instead, they are left to get on with pressured social lives, rife with competition and little individually tailored input from teachers, preachers, neighbors or even relatives.

When I subsequently served as a dean in a Cambridge College, I witnessed new trends whereby young people were increasingly keen to label themselves with “special” needs. These involved a host of adjustments, from extra time for examinations and dedicated teaching tools to demands for modifying the entire syllabus to avoid “triggering” bad feelings. This was a time, too, when diagnoses of disabilities were rising rapidly. With more extensive screening for disabilities and broadening diagnostic criteria, the number of young people identified as dyslexic grew to more than 20 times from the baseline recorded in the 1990s by 2015, while cases of autism increased by 175 percent between 2011 and 2022. [1]

Like many people in educational institutions, I worried that young people were seeking a formal assessment of disability partly to obtain in-group status with a distinctive set and partly to demand additional input from their teachers. There was a risk that instead of taking on the task of learning how to learn, how to communicate and interact, how to accept the variability of their talents, young people were now primed to outsource their challenges, demanding that others make adjustments to spoon-feed and coddle them. As an increasing number of their peers sought more input and adjustments, it was common to feel that being mainstream or neurotypical meant being left out.

The UK government, concerned about the rise in young people’s mental health needs, ordered an investigation of young people’s mental health and appointed Peter Fonagy, clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England, to lead the research. I anticipated that the report would show that ordinary difficult feelings—anxiety, frustration, stress, pressure, uncertainty—were all too often pathologized as disorders or conditions when the best approach would be to support young people to manage normal ups and downs of human emotions.

The review of young people’s mental health showed something very different and has prompted another shift in my perspective—not because of my previous concern that some mental health and disability diagnoses are too broad, but because the charge of overdiagnosis, while valid, clouds the main issue that there has been a significant rise in mental distress among young people. This is affecting both boys and girls, but from the age of 12, the impact on girls is greater. The close-up view is heartbreaking: many young people struggle with anxiety so powerful that they find school intolerable. Some are too depressed to sleep or eat, and some feel their lives are “not worth living.” [2]

In reflecting on the report, Peter Fonagy said, “I am in awe of their courage. Young people are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced. They are not fragile. They are outnumbered.”

The new UK review complements the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2023 report finding that nearly three out of five teen girls experience persistent sadness, double that in boys. [3] Misery and a sense of being weird, disliked, and also very special might be a signature element of adolescence, but today’s adolescence is crushing our children, who inhabit a digital ecosystem that inflicts persistent social comparison and self-doubt, socioeconomic instability and a precarious future, and a fractured support system that incentivizes the search for a special diagnosis because that is the route through which they might begin to get professional support.

I have circled back to my conviction that we need to offer sympathy and understanding and proactive support to young people—in the home, in school and in the community—to meet their core needs for autonomy (confidence in navigating risk), competence (skills to succeed academically and socially), and relatedness (belonging, community and purpose). Only with our support will these challenged generations of youth discover resilience.

1. Apter, T. (2001) The Myth of Maturity: What Teenagers Need from Parent to become Adults. New York: W.W. Norton.

2. Fonagy, P. (2026) Independent review into prevalence and support for mental health conditions, ADHD and autism. London: Department of Health and Social Care/UK Government.

3. Federal interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics. (2023). America's Children: Key National Indicators of Well-Being. U.S. Government Printing Office.

#4900. Sykeruns X7 electric dirt bike review: A lot of power for surprisingly little money

The mini electric dirt bike market has exploded over the last few years, with seemingly countless new brands offering everything from pint-sized electric pit bikes to surprisingly powerful off-road machines. The Sykeruns X7 falls somewhere in the middle, offering enough power to get into some serious trouble while keeping the price relatively approachable.

I’ve spent some time now riding the X7, and while it certainly isn’t the most refined electric dirt bike I’ve tested, there’s enough to like about what you’re getting for the money.

In fact, if you’re looking for a reasonably powerful electric dirt bike for recreational trail riding without spending several thousand dollars, this might be worth a closer look.

The Sykeruns X7 is a compact electric dirt bike featuring a 5,500W peak-rated motor, which translates to around 7.4 horsepower. That’s quite a bit of power for a bike at this price point of $1,699, especially considering that many similarly priced electric two-wheelers are significantly less powerful. Oh, and for our readers, we’ve gotten you set up with a 20% discount. Just use code ELECTREK20 to drop the price down to an impressive $1,359!

Sykeruns claims a top speed of 57 mph (92 km/h), though since this is an off-road only bike, you’ll rarely get the chance to put that claim to the test. I certainly didn’t, as I didn’t have a long enough and flat enough stretch of trail where I felt comfortable hitting nearly highway speeds on a low-cost e-moto.

The battery is a 60V 27Ah pack, providing 1,620 Wh of capacity. Sykeruns claims up to 60 miles (96 km) of range, though as with virtually every electric dirt bike, your actual range will depend heavily on how aggressively you’re riding. Fast trail riding, steep climbs, and repeated hard acceleration can eat through battery capacity much more quickly than leisurely cruising. Suffice it to say that you’ll likely not see the 60 mile figure in real world scenarios, but that’s still a fairly large battery.

The bike rolls on a 17-inch front wheel and 14-inch rear wheel, both wrapped in knobby off-road tires. Hydraulic disc brakes handle stopping duties, while an inverted suspension fork and rear monoshock help smooth out the bumps.

At 143 lb (65 kg), the X7 isn’t exactly featherweight, but it’s also far from being a full-size electric motorcycle.

The first thing I was surprised about with the X7 is that it offers a pretty decent amount of performance for the money. There’s enough power here to have some real fun, and the bike doesn’t feel like one of those underpowered mini electric motorcycles that struggles once you get beyond casual neighborhood speeds.

That said, I wouldn’t describe the acceleration as mind-blowing, either. We’re not talking about the kind of explosive power delivery you’d get from a high-end electric dirt bike costing several times as much. Instead, the X7 delivers a healthy amount of acceleration that feels appropriate for a recreational off-road machine.

And let’s be real here, that’s probably what most people shopping in this budget category are looking for.

The suspension is another area where the X7 earns a passing grade without necessarily winning any awards. The front fork and rear shock do their jobs, absorbing the bumps and ruts you’d expect to encounter on typical trails. It’s nothing I’d call plush, but I could see it doing light jumps with minimal air time.

Would I want to take this thing to a motocross track and start launching it off massive jumps? Not particularly. The suspension doesn’t have the premium feel or sophisticated damping of more expensive machines.

But for general trail riding, exploring dirt roads, and the occasional overlanding shenanigans, it’s perfectly serviceable. Not every electric dirt bike needs to be a competition-ready machine, and the X7 seems comfortable occupying that more recreational category.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the tires, which seem well suited to the bike’s intended purpose. The knobby tread offers a reasonable amount of grip for off-road riding, and I didn’t find myself immediately wishing for a tire upgrade.

The overall size is worth mentioning, too. This isn’t a particularly large electric dirt bike, but at my modest 5’7” (170 cm) height, I felt comfortable on it. The riding position didn’t feel overly cramped, and the bike was manageable enough that I didn’t feel like I was wrestling with an oversized machine.

Taller riders might find it a bit more compact than they’d prefer, but for average-height riders, the proportions seem reasonable.

If there’s one area where the X7 reminds you of its budget-friendly $1,699 price tag, it’s the overall level of refinement.

Nothing about the bike struck me as particularly premium. The components, finishes, and general construction are more in line with what I’d expect from a relatively inexpensive electric dirt bike.

But that’s not necessarily a criticism. There’s a difference between something feeling inexpensive and something feeling inadequate, and the X7 generally stays on the acceptable side of that line.

The controls are straightforward, the digital display provides the basic information you need, and the overall package feels focused on delivering usable performance rather than impressing riders with fancy features.

The grippy hydraulic brakes are also a welcome inclusion, especially considering the speeds this bike is capable of reaching. With a machine that can approach highway speeds, having proper motorcycle-style braking hardware is important.

Of course, long-term durability is a separate question. Budget electric dirt bikes don’t always have the same track record, parts availability, or established dealer networks as the more recognizable motorcycle brands. That’s something worth considering before purchasing, particularly if you plan to ride hard or frequently.

One thing I appreciate about the Sykeruns X7 is that the company makes its intended use fairly clear.

There’s a large red warning sticker on the bike explaining that it’s intended for off-road use only. That’s a good thing, especially in today’s market, where the lines between electric bicycles, electric dirt bikes, and electric motorcycles are becoming increasingly blurred, despite laws existing to keep these types of bikes out of the bike lane and off of public roads.

The X7 is absolutely not an electric bicycle. It doesn’t have pedals, it produces several thousand watts of power, and it’s capable of speeds far beyond anything permitted under electric bicycle regulations.

It’s an off-road electric motorcycle, plain and simple.

Interestingly, though, Sykeruns has equipped the bike with features like a tail light and turn signals, which could potentially give some riders the wrong impression.

Those are certainly useful features on a motorcycle, but they don’t magically make a vehicle street legal. Without the necessary certification, registration, and other road-use requirements, the X7 remains an off-road-only machine.

I worry that some buyers might see those lights and assume they can ride the bike around town like a small electric motorcycle. That’s not the case, and it’s important to understand that distinction before buying one.

After spending time with the Sykeruns X7, my biggest takeaway is that this is a reasonably capable electric dirt bike at a pretty compelling price.

It’s not the best electric dirt bike I’ve ever ridden. The suspension is fairly basic, the build quality is unremarkable, and there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about the design.

But for $1,699 (or $1,359 if you use the code ELECTREK20 to take 20% off!), you’re getting a 5.5 kW peak-rated electric motorcycle with a sizable battery, proper off-road tires, hydraulic brakes, and enough performance to have some genuine fun on the trails.

I wouldn’t say that the X7 here is trying to compete with more up-market electric dirt bikes from the likes of Juiced, Sur-Ron or Talaria on overall refinement, but they make this type of riding much more accessible.

And that’s really where I think the X7 makes the most sense.

If you’re an experienced dirt bike rider looking for a highly refined machine with excellent suspension and premium components, you’ll probably want to keep shopping.

But if you’re someone who wants a fun electric dirt bike for exploring private property, cruising around trails where motorized riding is permitted, or just enjoying some recreational off-road riding without spending a fortune, the Sykeruns X7 offers a pretty reasonable package.

It doesn’t need to be amazing at everything. At this price, being pretty good at most things is already an accomplishment.

#4899. Heart Failure Is Becoming More Common in Adults Under 65, Report Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

An estimated 56 million people worldwide were living with heart failure in 2023, more than double the number in 1990, according to a new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analysis published September 30 in JAMA Cardiology.

Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs. Despite its name, heart failure doesn’t mean the heart has stopped beating.

A separate 2026 report from the Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) found that heart failure contributed to more than 450,000 deaths in the United States in 2023, with particularly sharp increases in mortality among adults under 65.

Approximately 7.7 million U.S. adults (3%) are living with heart failure, according to the HFSA report. That number is projected to rise to 8.7 million by 2030, 10.3 million by 2040, and 11.4 million by 2050.

The GBD researchers said the findings highlight the growing burden of heart failure associated with population growth and aging, as well as the need for prevention and treatment strategies targeting common causes such as ischemic heart disease and hypertension (high blood pressure).

Between 2010 and 2022, heart failure hospitalization rates increased among adults under 65 while declining among those 65 and older. Between 2001 and 2020, estimated heart failure mortality rates more than doubled among adults ages 25 to 44 and nearly doubled among those ages 45 to 64.

“I think we’re seeing the impact of cardiovascular risk factors developing earlier in life. Conditions such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and sleep apnea are affecting younger adults at higher rates than in previous generations,” Kevin Shah, MD, Program Director of Heart Failure Outreach at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the analysis, told Healthline.

“When those risk factors are present for decades, they can eventually lead to heart failure at a younger age,” he said.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist at Manhattan Cardiology in New York City who was also not involved in the analysis, noted that improvements in early detection may also play a role.

“Our tools to detect early heart failure are also improving with time, and as a result, patients may receive an earlier diagnosis and can hopefully start medical therapy to prevent progression or possibly even reverse the process entirely.”

Heart failure contributed to 452,573 deaths in the United States in 2023, accounting for approximately 14.6% of all deaths that year, according to the HFSA report.

Age-adjusted heart failure mortality rates increased by approximately 37% between 2010 and 2023, with preliminary 2024 data suggesting the upward trend is continuing.

This increase appears to have reversed more than a decade of previous progress in reducing heart failure mortality.

Ischemic heart disease and hypertension were among the most common causes of heart failure in older adults, according to the GBD report. However, the underlying causes varied considerably by age group and region.

Among children and young adults, congenital heart abnormalities and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common causes of heart failure. Heart failure associated with alcohol use was most prevalent during middle adulthood.

The analysis also identified regional differences in the underlying causes of heart failure:

The global burden of heart failure is expected to grow as populations age.

While not all cases of heart failure can be prevented, managing certain risk factors can help reduce your risk. These include:

According to Shah, other important steps to help prevent heart failure include maintaining a healthy weight, staying physically active, and managing conditions such as diabetes and high cholesterol.

He added that regular medical care is important because many of these risk factors can be identified and treated long before heart failure develops.

“Heart failure is often treatable and may even be reversible with early diagnosis and treatment. It is important for patients to seek help early if they have concerning symptoms, such as exertional shortness of breath, chest pain, leg swelling, or anything else they’re concerned about. Talk with your doctors early and often,” said Blumfield.

#4898. The Mustache Was Never the Point of Movember

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

The first time I showed up to a GORUCK training day was not long after I finished my first Ironman. I didn’t go looking for it. A friend from work dared me.

GORUCK is an endurance event where you pack a backpack full of bricks and take on challenges. Some involve getting cold, wet, and sandy. Others involve carrying odd-shaped objects around. The real events start at 10 p.m. and run until the sun comes up.

The training day was in daylight at Baker Beach in San Francisco, and it was all dudes. We had the same curiosity and the same burning desire to see what we were made of. We also wanted to find other knuckleheads who think spending time in the ocean at 2 a.m. is perfectly normal. Dare I say, fun.

What I didn’t know at the time was that some of the men I met on that beach would still be good friends of mine 14 years later. I wrote about those friendships in “The Power of Crucible Events to Solidify Male Friendships.”

That got me thinking about the origins of Movember.

In 2003, two friends in Melbourne, Travis Garone and Luke Slattery, were having a beer at the Gypsy Bar in Fitzroy. The conversation drifted to fashion trends that keep coming back. They started wondering where the mustache had gone.

So they decided to bring it back. Travis emailed their friends with a subject line that doubled as a dare: “Are you man enough to be my man?”

There was no cause that first year. No fundraising page. No awareness campaign. Just 30 men growing mustaches for a month.

The cause came the next year, when the group decided to grow for men’s health. Today, millions of men around the world take part.

Co-founder Adam Garone put it plainly: “Movember itself started with friends getting together, growing Mo’s and having fun.”

That’s the part that gets lost. Movember didn’t start as a health campaign that happened to involve friends. It started as a group of friends who happened to build a health campaign.

There’s a popular idea that men’s friendships are broken because men won’t open up. If guys would just talk about their feelings, the theory goes, the loneliness would lift.

Tyler Austin Harper isn’t buying it. Writing in The Atlantic, he argued that the real crisis of male friendship comes from something else. Men haven’t lost the ability to connect. They’ve lost the shared activities they connect through.

That fits what I’ve seen. Men don’t usually become friends sitting across a table and sharing. They become friends standing next to each other, doing something side by side.

It also takes time. A lot of it. University of Kansas researcher Jeffrey Hall estimates it takes 40 to 60 hours to form a casual friendship, and more than 200 hours to become good friends. And not all hours count the same. Hanging out and joking around builds friendship. Working together counts for much less.

That’s the hidden genius of a dumb challenge. It gives you hours together that feel like play. Nobody on that training day was on the clock. Nobody was networking. We were a bunch of guys carrying bricks around a beach because we wanted to.

A month of growing a mustache works the same way. It’s time with your friends you’d never think to schedule. It also shows your care for your fellow men.

This year’s campaign is built around a simple message: Connection doesn’t have to be a big heart-to-heart.

As Movember’s marketing director, Helena Jennison, put it, “Connection doesn’t always have to start with a difficult conversation.” Sometimes it’s a laugh. Sometimes it’s a shared interest. Sometimes it’s growing a mustache.

It works. According to Movember’s own research, two in five people who took part made a new social connection through it.

The charity funds the same idea year-round. In Newcastle, England, a program called Men’s Pie Club starts from a simple premise. Men like eating pies. So they learn to make them together. The conversations come later, as the men get to know each other.

Look at what’s going on in each of these. Nobody signs up for “emotional connection.” They sign up for a mustache, a pie, a beach full of bricks. The activity is the excuse. The friendship is what they actually came for, even if they’d never say so.

Men need a reason to be in the same place at the same time. Give them one, and they’ll usually take it from there.

You don’t need a cause to start. You need a dare.

Here are three ways to find yours this month.

In my book, The Male Friendship Experience, I call these friendship missions: shared activities that give men a reason to show up, again and again. The mission matters less than the showing up.

Fourteen years ago, a work friend dared me to go carry bricks on a beach. I went to train. I found the men I’d later stand beside in the dark Pacific at 2 a.m. Those same men still stand by me on great days and dark days.

#4896. BMW is going upscale with its first 3-row EV, the iX7

BMW’s next electric SUV won’t just be bigger. The iX7 will sit at the top of the brand’s EV lineup when it debuts in 2027, bringing a more luxurious option to the mix.

After the new X5 and iX5, the X7, BMW’s biggest SUV, is due for a Neue Klasse overhaul. BMW said the second-generation X7 will arrive in 2027, including the first fully electric version, the iX7.

Ahead of its upcoming debut, camouflaged prototypes have been spotted testing, revealing a few design changes.

Although it won’t fully adopt BMW’s Neue Klasse design, like the iX3, the three-row SUV appears to feature a slimmer, more upright Kidney Grille instead of the traditional wide BMW Grille.

The iX7 also swaps conventional pull-style door handles for small handles on the vehicle’s pillar. It also retains split headlights rather than the updated Neue Klasse-style headlights on the iX3 (shown below on the right).

While BMW has yet to reveal details, a Reddit user who claims to work at BMW’s factory in South Carolina and has seen the second-generation X7 shared a few new details.

Like the X5 and iX5, the new X7 and iX7 will retain a more traditional design rather than going full-on Neue Klasse, including the Kidney Grille. The user also said BMW is dropping the split tailgate, which it did with the new X5, in favor of a standard one-piece tailgate.

Inside, the dashboard and center console are similar to the new X5, but with upgraded tech and features from the new 7 Series sedan.

BMW said the new 7 Series sedan “takes the lead when it comes to the introduction of technologies from the Neue Klasse into existing models.”

Optional features will reportedly include the upgraded 31.3″ 8K BMW Theatre Screen for rear passengers and a 14.6″ BMW Passenger Screen. It will also have optional touch screen panels on the rear doors, the user said.

While most of the claims make sense, we’ll have to wait for BMW to confirm it officially. The new X7 and iX7 are expected to debut in mid-2027.

Like the iX5 60 xDrive, the three-row iX7 is expected to use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain. The iX5’s AWD setup delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, enabling it to hit 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds.

The iX5 uses a massive 144 kWh battery, which BMW said offers up to 435 miles of range. It will also use an 800V electrical system for fast charging.

BMW showed just how fast it can charge during a media event in Southern California earlier this month, where the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW. With up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes, BMW says.

The new X7 and iX7 are expected to go into production at BMW’s Spartanburg plant in SC in late 2027, joining the new iX5.

#4895. Viola Davis Says Shingles Pain Was a ‘9 Out of 10’: How It Changed Her Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award-winning actress and producer Viola Davis was 50 years old and at the height of her career when she developed shingles.

“All of a sudden, I got a rash in the middle of traveling and juggling [back-to-back] movies that started in the middle of my stomach [and] wrapped around my back,” she told Healthline. “And the pain was definitely at a 9 out of 10.”

Focused on work, Davis didn’t see a doctor right away. Her symptoms eventually subsided but later returned on her upper back.

“That is when I was like, ‘Oh, my goodness, I just got bitten by a poisonous spider,” said Davis. “It felt like really bad nerve pain…then someone mentioned the word shingles.”

After seeing a doctor, Davis learned she had shingles, which is caused by the same virus responsible for chickenpox. She also learned that the risk increases with age as the immune system naturally weakens.

“It can also lead to herpetic neuralgia, lifelong pain that can result from a shingles outbreak,” Robyn Liu, MD, member of the board of directors at the American Academy of Family Physicians, told Healthline.

Shingles can affect daily life, including work and sleep.

“Many people don’t realize that shingles can be associated with nerve pain, and for some, that pain can last for months or even years after the rash has resolved due to potential long-term complications,” Jennifer Caudle, DO, family medicine physician and associate professor at Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine, told Healthline.

Nearly one in three people in the U.S. develops shingles in their lifetime.

“Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, but the risk goes up as we age,” said Liu.

After learning about shingles, Davis said she realized that she could no longer ignore her body.

“You just cannot. I mean, I know that people say it at nauseam, but, for me, it meant slowing down,” she said. “But then the shingles slowed me down…even though I was getting up, I was working out, [the] pain and the sluggishness was awful.”

Now 61, Davis has teamed up with GSK for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to raise awareness about shingles.

“[I’m] sending the message out there for women to really honor themselves and honor their bodies,” she said. “Their bodies literally speak. They’re the other character in their lives.”

After her experience with shingles, Davis began scheduling regular annual checkups.

“Before that time, I did absolutely go to my doctor, but only when it was absolutely necessary, you know, to get my colonoscopy, get my mammogram, but I never went if something felt odd,” said Davis.

Now, whenever she feels off, she doesn’t hesitate to see her doctor. She makes it a point to be honest with them about what’s going on with her body, and she is not shy about asking questions.

“I feel that it’s my job. It’s what I owe myself, and not only [do] I owe myself, it’s what I owe my daughter, it’s what I owe my husband, it’s what I owe my elderly mom, who is in advanced dementia [and] I take care of her,” Davis said.

Caudle stressed the importance of bringing questions to your doctor.

“That’s what we’re here for. Sometimes patients ​tell me they don’t realize they can ask questions or introduce a topic that their healthcare provider didn’t bring up first,” she said. “But a simple question like, ‘Am I at risk for shingles?’ can be a great place to begin.”

Davis has made stress reduction a priority. When she developed shingles, she was juggling an intense workload and adjusting to life as a new mom after adopting her daughter.

“I was someone who just ignored stress,” said Davis. “[When] we meet each other, it becomes a contest: Who can work through their stress the best? I felt like I had to strike while the iron was hot.”

Today, Davis makes stress reduction a priority through activities such as spraying her pillows with lavender, taking Epsom salt baths, meditating, going to therapy, exercising, spending time outdoors, using vagus nerve stimulation, and connecting with family and friends.

“It’s like I overdo it now because I feel like I have to overdo it in order to compete with my schedule. But that’s what I owe myself,” Davis said.

Still, her profession can be intense and time consuming due to shooting and promotional schedules. She still makes time to de-stress and focuses on projects that bring her joy.

“Your career is only as important as how much you enjoy it; how much it adds to your life,” said Davis. “[For] me, it used to be something that I felt defined my worth. I don’t feel like it defines my worth now…I feel that I’m already worthy… I was born worthy. That’s how I see it.”

Vaccination is the best way to protect against shingles, Liu said. The shingles vaccine is more than 90% effective at preventing the disease.

“For children, that protection begins with the chickenpox vaccine, which can be given along with other routine childhood immunizations. Preventing chickenpox also lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life,” she said.

Liu recommends two doses of the shingles vaccine for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems.

“Some patients may have more questions because side effects can be more noticeable than with other vaccines, so it’s important to understand the tradeoff: short-term discomfort from the vaccine versus the risk of lasting complications from shingles,” said Liu.

Side effects may include headache or redness, swelling, itching, and soreness where the shot was given.

“I tell my patients that these reactions are common and usually clear up within a day or two. They’re a normal sign that your body is building protection,” said Liu.

#4894. The Manosphere Got Men Into the Gym. Now What?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

For many men, the gym isn’t just training; it’s identity management. It’s one of the few places where they can reliably feel agency, strength, and self-respect.

The manosphere, a nebulous grouping of male influencers, podcasts, and content creators, has tapped into those desires, turning physical self-improvement into an entry point for creating male followers. The popularity of manosphere influencers has proven that boys and men want to be strong. That can be a good thing. But, what often happens next is more troubling.

In my experience, most men don’t need convincing to pay attention to their bodies. They want bodies they’re proud of. They want to feel capable, disciplined, and desirable.

The issue is how some influencers shape men's relationship with their bodies into a competition of muscle, performance, and status. Men searching for content to improve their health and fitness can easily become inundated by messages that promote obsession, perfectionism, and body dysmorphia.

Andrew Tate, the manosphere’s most notorious influencer, has said that missing one gym session won’t hurt you, but “the attitude that allows you to miss one session without guilt” will. In other words, you should feel guilty for not working out. It makes you weak—less of a man.

There are two common responses to this messaging.

The first is to dismiss it as toxic nonsense. Why would you listen to someone like that?

But dismissing the manosphere misses the point. There's something men are looking for online, and shaming them for what they admire can deepen their attachment to it. We need to acknowledge the real positive changes in men who have started lifting or eating better because of manosphere influencers.

The second response is to offer a supposedly better reason to exercise: do it for others. Two years ago, I argued that men should take care of themselves not just for their own sake, but for their partners and families.

When men neglect their health, the consequences don’t stop with them. Their partners often end up carrying more of the emotional, physical, and financial burden. Self-care is, in that sense, a form of responsibility. I still believe that.

But putting all the emphasis on what a man’s fitness does for others can reinforce the expectation that a man's body doesn't really matter. It's a machine whose value lies in what it can produce. When fitness is for others, it loses its intrinsic value and becomes another performance.

What if we stopped trying to replace men’s desire to be strong and fit, and instead helped them build a healthier relationship with that motivation?

Wanting to be strong is different from believing you’re worthless when you’re weak. Wanting to be attractive is different from needing to outrank other men. Choosing discipline is different from being unable to tolerate a day of rest. The manosphere often misses all of these.

And here’s what I see most clearly in my coaching work: men may feel more comfortable treating their bodies like machines that need maintenance than companions that deserve care. It's not that men don't want to care for their bodies. It's that they've never been taught how. They've never been allowed to be more yielding, gentle, or nurturing to themselves. All they know is push, force, and domination.

If we want to help men keep fitness in their lives without dominating their bodies, measuring themselves against every man in the gym, or objectifying themselves (and others), we need to change the culture that says your worth depends on your rank, rest is weakness, and other men are competition.

If you're a man who wants to work out, ask yourself:

These questions help men be honest about the pressure they feel to look or perform a rigid notion of masculinity. But the work doesn't stop there. Men need other men who can model mature forms of strength and help change the narrative that strength and vulnerability are opposites.

These interactions can happen on sports teams, in running clubs, or in a well-facilitated men’s group. Or they can come from a coach, a therapist, or a friend who can say “enough” without being seen as weak. These experiences help men get comfortable with displaying strength without domination. Over time, the exercise persists and something subtle shifts:

None of this requires a man to stop wanting to be strong, attractive, or respected. Those desires simply no longer have to decide his worth.

If a young man in your life is watching this content, try asking what about these influencers resonates with him. What do they seem to understand about his life that other adults miss? Is it discipline? A sense of purpose? Men to look up to?

Honor that motive. Then help him find a healthier place to pursue it.

He already wants to work out. What gets built next is the whole story.

#4893. Waymo adds nearly 250 square miles of robotaxi coverage in 5 cities

Waymo is growing its driverless service area by nearly 250 square miles over the next week, spread across Los Angeles, Nashville, Orlando, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

That’s about as big as Tesla’s entire Houston Robotaxi geofence after this week’s expansion, and Waymo is adding it in cities where it already runs with nobody in the driver’s seat.

The company announced the expansion in a short post on its blog today. Here’s what changes in each market, with Waymo’s updated service area maps:

Service now runs down the coast into the South Bay, through Manhattan Beach and Redondo Beach to Torrance.

The zone pushes further south, and riders can now get to the zoo.

Coverage on the east side nearly doubles, and there’s more service downtown.

The service area now stretches north to La Jolla, taking in University City and Clairemont along the way.

Waymo is pushing further into the South Bay, including a connection to BART at Berryessa station in San Jose. The service area now runs from San Francisco down the Peninsula to San Jose and Campbell.

Waymo didn’t break out square mileage by city, and it didn’t say how many vehicles it’s adding to cover the new ground. The updated maps are already in the Waymo app.

Some of these markets are very young. Waymo opened Nashville to public riders in April with a zone of about 60 square miles covering downtown, Midtown, Music Row, and East Nashville. San Diego only went public on September 1, with roughly 50 square miles between the beach and I-15 that barely crossed north of I-8. So getting to La Jolla less than two months later is a big jump.

In May, Waymo pushed its coverage past 1,400 square miles across 11 cities, which is bigger than the state of Rhode Island. Since then, it went driverless in Las Vegas, launched San Diego, and now says it operates in 15 US metros with more than 500,000 paid rides per week. It’s even mapping Toronto for a 2028 launch.

Tesla is also drawing bigger maps. After launching Robotaxi in Dallas and Houston with tiny geofences in April, it stretched Houston to about 254 square miles this week, according to Robotaxi Tracker. But the tracker counts 34 vehicles in Houston.

I'd like to see Waymo add more airports to their service list. Airports are huge drivers of both ride count and revenue for ride services. Waymo currently serves airports in some of their cities, such as Phoenix, San Francisco, and Nashville. However, other major airports such as LAX, Atlanta, and Dallas/Fort Worth do not currently have terminal service even though Waymo operates in those cities. Adding these might not look flashy on a map, but it would be a huge addition to Waymo's bottom line.

And on the metric that reflects actual use, it’s not close. Waymo logged 3.9 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026, while Tesla’s driverless fleet did 558,000 miles in its latest reported week, mostly in Austin. That’s about 7x, and it comes on the same day Elon Musk claimed the robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest.”

I like this. Good progress. But I’ll be truly impressed when the Bay Area service area extends south into LA, expands north, and the same happens in San Diego.

It’s going to happen. Waymo is already dabbling with highway operations in California.I can see them linking all those service areas within the next 2 years. Maybe even by the end of next year if all goes well.

#4892. Rivian electric van spotted in Walmart+ livery, hinting at a fleet deal

A Rivian electric delivery van wrapped in Walmart+ branding was photographed on a car hauler on I-94 in northwest Indiana today. It’s the first public sign that Walmart could become Rivian’s next big van customer after Amazon.

Neither company has announced a deal. But Walmart’s last two electric van suppliers are out of the business, and Rivian is one of the few companies still building a purpose-built electric delivery van in the US.

Reddit user biggie_ballzzz posted the photo to r/RIVNstock this afternoon, asking if anyone had heard about a partnership. The van is strapped to a multi-car trailer between two Ford pickups, with a big “Walmart+” logo on the side and “Same day. Right to your door.” on the rear doors.

There’s no mistaking the vehicle. It’s Rivian’s Commercial Van, with the same tall body and red light bar wrapping around the rear that you see on Amazon Prime vans everywhere.

A few commenters suspected an AI image, but there’s no clear evidence. In fact, a second commenter then shared a photo of a van in the same livery parked in front of a Walmart Supercenter in Hammond, Indiana, about 30 miles to the west.

Rivian (RIVN) stock was up more than 3% this afternoon as the photo made the rounds, according to screenshots shared in the thread. That’s two days before Rivian reports its Q3 2026 results on Thursday, October 29.

Walmart has been trying to electrify last-mile delivery for years. Its supplier picks haven’t aged well.

In 2022, it signed up to buy 4,500 Canoo vans and put them to work on InHome deliveries. Canoo filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in January 2025 and ceased operations.

The same year, Walmart reserved 5,000 BrightDrop vans from GM, and officially added them to its delivery fleet in late 2024. Then GM killed BrightDrop production at its CAMI plant in Ontario a year ago, with no plan to build the van anywhere else. BrightDrop was on pace for roughly 4,000 US sales in 2025, compared to more than 60,000 for GM’s gas-powered Express and Savana vans.

So Walmart is running two orphaned EV van platforms. And if it wants more purpose-built electric vans at scale, the list of US options is very short.

Amazon ordered 100,000 vans from Rivian, and its fleet has now passed 40,000 units on the road. But the deal came with an exclusivity period that ended in November 2023, and Rivian has struggled to land anything close to Amazon-scale since.

AT&T signed up for a pilot in late 2023, and HelloFresh came on board in 2025. In February 2025, Rivian opened van sales to any business, with the RCV 500 starting at $79,900 and the larger RCV 700 at $83,900. None of those customers moves the needle like Walmart would.

There’s also a charging angle. Walmart now operates its own 400 kW fast-charging network at 100 stores in 20 states, and its manager of retail charging, Wade Higgins, previously worked at Rivian, according to his bio on the board of Minnesota car-sharing nonprofit HOURCAR.

One van on a trailer isn’t a fleet order. Not yet, anyway. This could be a test unit for a pilot program, like the one AT&T announced in 2023. And since Rivian sells vans to any business now, Walmart could have simply bought a few to try them out.

So Walmart is running two orphaned EV van platforms. And if it wants more purpose-built electric vans at scale, the list of US options is very short.

Walmart also runs Ford E-Transit vans but I can't find recent numbers for how many

But the timing makes sense. Walmart bet on Canoo and GM, and both left it with vans nobody builds anymore. If you’re Walmart and you want to keep electrifying same-day delivery, Rivian is the obvious call. Its plant in Normal, Illinois, has already built tens of thousands of these vans, and the platform has been proven at scale by the one company Walmart is trying to beat on delivery.

That’s the awkward part. Walmart putting its brand on the same van as Amazon Prime is a bit funny, and it says a lot about how thin the electric van market has gotten in the US.

For Rivian, a Walmart deal would matter. The van business gives it volume in Normal while R2 ramps, and it badly needs proof that the van isn’t just an Amazon product. We’ll see if Rivian says anything on Thursday’s call. We wouldn’t bet on a massive order announcement, but a Walmart pilot wouldn’t surprise us one bit.

#4891. The Liver Does a Lot for Your Body. Here Are 8 Ways to Return the Favor.

Skip the herbal detoxes and follow these doctor-backed tips instead.

YOUR LARGEST INTERNAL organ is a master at multitasking. You can think of it as a refinery. Everything you consume—from your breakfast burrito to any medication you take—your liver filters, processes, stores, and/or turns into something new (it even makes cholesterol). The organ also puts in the hard work of regulating glucose, which involves holding on to that sugar and then deploying it when your body needs energy. And your liver helps handle the dirty work of sending whatever you don’t need out into the toilet.

ALL OF THE FACTORS below get in the way of your liver doing all of its jobs—and eventually prevent it from doing any of them. These drive the first stage of liver disease, which is inflammation. The second stage is called fibrosis, which occurs when chronic inflammation leads to liver scarring. In the third stage, cirrhosis, the refinery starts to function less efficiently. When cirrhosis goes too far, your liver begins to shut down, and eventually you’ll need a liver transplant.

The five main types are lettered A through E. In North America, A, B, and C are the most common, but A is typically mild. You used to hear a lot more about hepatitis B and C because they can lead to cirrhosis and even cancer—but they’re not the threat they once were (see more about that below).

Technically, your liver dies a little bit every time it processes alcohol. If you drink too much and kill too many liver cells, the liver has difficulty performing all its functions. Fat accumulates, and trouble is on its way.

Formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease is a fatty liver caused by things other than alcohol. The biggest culprits are obesity and type 2 diabetes. MASLD affects about 30 percent of people in the world, and cases are rising in the U.S.

YOU'LL NEED A doctor’s help. The severe symptoms you associate with liver problems—including yellowing eyes and skin (jaundice), swelling of the abdomen, or confusion—show up only when your liver is failing, says Richard Sterling, MD, hepatologist at Virginia Commonwealth University. Earlier symptoms, like fatigue, are so vague that liver trouble is tough to self-diagnose. A standard comprehensive blood panel, like the one you get with your annual physical, can measure the health of your liver and indicate a possible problem. The tests check liver enzymes (high is bad), platelet count (low is bad), albumin (you want high), total protein (low is bad), and bilirubin (high isn’t great). The panel should also include screenings for hepatitis B and C.

“WHEN PATIENTS COME to see me, they’re really scared,” says Rohit Loomba, MD, director of the MASLD Research Center at UC San Diego, because they think liver trouble is a death sentence. That’s not true anymore. “In the last two decades, we’ve completely revolutionized the treatment of liver problems,” Dr. Loomba says. Four positives:

Fibrosis that hasn’t advanced all the way to cirrhosis can be reversed, starting with removing the cause of the problem (by improving diet, avoiding alcohol). Even cirrhosis can be stabilized under the care of a liver specialist.

Better screening plus vaccines for hepatitis A and B have made viral hepatitis less common. Now there are good drugs for hepatitis B and ones that can basically cure hepatitis C.

The FDA approved Rezdiffra, the first drug for treating an advanced stage of MASLD called MASH, also formerly NASH. (Don’t ask.) And everyone’s favorite wonder drugs—GLP-1 inhibitors—may swoop in here too: Dr. Loomba published research that shows taking Mounjaro for a year was effective in treating MASH. Other semaglutide drugs might also work. In 2025, the FDA approved the use of Wegovy to treat MASH in adults with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis.

All cancers are scary, but liver cancer is one that may be preventable. For the most part, you only develop the disease once you’ve done extensive damage to the organ. If you get screened when you need it and adjust your lifestyle to keep your liver happy, you can limit your cancer risk.

Lean protein. Lots of produce. Little sugar. All easy on the liver.

A recommended 150 minutes per week at moderate intensity can help reduce liver inflammation and rid the organ of fat.

Antioxidants and other compounds in coffee (even decaf) may help protect against fibrosis. While studies may vary, researchers suggest positive effects start at two to three cups a day.

If you’re carrying extra pounds, losing 5 to 10 percent of your body weight could reduce fat in your liver by about 30 percent. Need some help? Check out MH’s four-week walking for weight loss plan.

Consume too much and your body converts it to fat that can build up in your liver. (This 30-day plan helps you cut back painlessly.)

Don’t stop taking them, but work with a doc to determine which ones can hurt your liver, especially if you’re drinking alcohol. Watch acetaminophen too: Even when taken as directed, it can cause liver damage if you drink to excess, says Dr. Sterling.

The best amount of alcohol for your liver: none. Realistically, though, when you drink, keep it to one or two and try not to do it daily. Note: Larger bodies can’t necessarily handle more. People with extra weight likely already have some liver damage that makes their body worse at processing booze.

These are unregulated, and some can be toxic to your liver; kava and herbal weight-loss supplements are two of the worst. And by the way, a “liver cleanse” or “liver detox”? “That’s not something we as hepatologists recommend,” says Dr. Sterling, “and I’m not aware of any data that say that that works.”

Kevin is a writer and editor living in Brooklyn. In past lives he’s been an economist, computer salesman, mathematician, barista, and college football equipment manager.

#4890. PMOS, Formerly PCOS, May Be Associated with Alzheimer's Disease Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), has been linked to changes in brain function and cognition that may overlap with those seen in Alzheimer’s disease.

However, a review published October 13 in the Journal of the Endocrine Society suggests that metabolic conditions commonly associated with PMOS, rather than PMOS itself, may help explain a potential link to Alzheimer’s disease and dementia risk.

“Researchers are exploring whether some metabolic conditions commonly seen in women with PMOS, such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, [and] elevated cholesterol, could play a role in dementia, since these are already known risk factors for cognitive decline,” Yesika Garcia, MD, board certified endocrinologist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline.

“In other words, any potential connection may be related to these underlying metabolic issues rather than PMOS itself. I think it’s important to clarify that an association does not mean causation,” she added.

The researchers searched PubMed for studies published through 2025 examining brain structure and function, cognitive performance, biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, and dementia risk in people with PMOS.

Because PMOS is a newer term, the researchers searched for studies using both PMOS and PCOS.

The review identified studies suggesting that people with PMOS may experience mild differences in certain cognitive abilities, including:

Some brain imaging studies using MRI and PET scans identified differences in brain structure and function among people with PMOS. Researchers also observed hormonal changes associated with differences in gray matter.

Some studies identified elevated biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease in people with PMOS. These findings appeared to overlap with metabolic changes seen in type 2 diabetes, particularly those associated with obesity and insulin resistance.

The researchers also found that neurological differences were less pronounced when people with PMOS were compared with metabolically healthy control groups, suggesting that associated metabolic conditions may play an important role in these findings.

Overall, the review suggests that metabolic conditions associated with PMOS may contribute to changes in brain health, although more research is needed to determine whether PMOS independently affects Alzheimer’s disease or dementia risk.

“I think we need to be careful about drawing conclusions too early. The research raises some good questions, but it doesn’t prove that PCOS [PMOS] causes Alzheimer’s disease,” said Dung Trinh, MD, internist, of MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“What it does reinforce is how important metabolic health may be when it comes to protecting our brains as we get older,” he added.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed. She also added that more attention and research need to be given to PMOS, brain changes, and future risks of dementia.

There are various ways that PMOS and dementia may share pathways and overlap, according to the researchers. Some of these shared pathways include:

Trinh explained that insulin resistance may be one of the most important connections between PMOS and dementia.

Although insulin is commonly associated with diabetes and blood sugar regulation, it also plays an important role in brain function. When insulin signaling doesn’t work properly, it may interfere with how brain cells use energy, potentially contributing to problems with memory and thinking over time.

Chronic inflammation, which can occur in people with PMOS, may also play a role in Alzheimer’s disease, Trinh told Healthline.

“Researchers are looking at how these metabolic changes may affect amyloid and tau, two proteins associated with Alzheimer’s. Some brain imaging studies have even found differences in brain structure and function among women with PCOS [PMOS],” he said.

Ross added that elevated androgen levels, which are common in people with PMOS, may also play a role in dementia risk.

“An important distinction is that these risk factors are not present in every woman with PMOS, and having PMOS does not automatically mean someone will experience cognitive decline,” cautioned Garcia.

Garcia noted that many of the dementia risk factors associated with PMOS are modifiable.

“Regular exercise, including both cardiovascular activity and strength training, can improve insulin sensitivity, help with weight management, and support cardiovascular and brain health,” she added.

“A Mediterranean-style diet, with plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean sources of protein, is a reasonable place to start,” he said.

Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure is also important, Trinh and Garcia noted.

“Medication, like metformin, can also improve insulin resistance, which may further reduce the risk of dementia,” Ross added.

Getting adequate sleep, avoiding smoking, and staying mentally and socially active are additional ways to support long-term brain health, Garcia told Healthline.

“For someone with PCOS [PMOS], I would encourage regular visits with their healthcare provider to monitor metabolic health and address problems early,” said Trinh.

“While we cannot say that these interventions specifically prevent dementia in women with PMOS, we know they benefit overall metabolic and cardiovascular health, which are closely connected to brain health,” explained Garcia.

#4889. You Can See Everything on the Surface, Not What Lies Beneath

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

I’m writing from the Hamptons. It’s the off-season, and the place feels like a small town, albeit a small town full of influential people, big thinkers, and, yes, some big egos. Almost everyone here is talking about You Can See Everything.

“Do you believe her? Aren’t her eyes crazy? Is she a narcissist? And what about her partner? Was he the real villain?”

It’s human nature to sort people into categories. We want to figure out what happened, so we won’t get fooled ourselves. We want a villain and a victim. We also want to feel better about ourselves, because at least we’re not “that crazy.” And it makes good theater.

If you haven’t seen the film: In the 34 days before Elizabeth Holmes reported to federal prison, she and her partner, Billy Evans, let a film crew led by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim record nearly every move. On the surface, the goal seemed to be showing them as everyday parents: raising their kids, walking on the beach, making eggs.

The title makes a promise: full access, nothing hidden, the real person behind the headlines at last.

The movie is disorienting. It took me a while to process. I won’t share all my thoughts here, but one has stayed with me: A camera can see everything on the surface. It can’t see the hidden drivers underneath.

A camera records behavior: what we say, how we stand, the stories we tell. It rarely captures the why. Under every polished performance and every bad decision, a hidden driver is steering. Unless you’re looking for it, you’ll miss it.

In my work as an executive coach, I use an assessment that uncovers these drivers and lays out the good, the bad, and the ugly in each one. I didn’t create it, and to be clear, it isn’t a personality test. It measures drive: the deep needs that push us forward.

I’ve never assessed Elizabeth Holmes, and I won’t guess at what drives her. But I have coached many founders and tech leaders, and her story reminds me of one of them. She happens to be a woman, but many men fall into the same trap. Her story shows what happens when hidden drivers go unseen.

From a distance, Laura had it all. She was brilliant, fast-moving, and, on paper, wildly successful. She carried herself as if she were the only one in the know and everyone else was slow to catch up.

When you asked her a question, she didn’t answer it. She used the moment to show how much more she knew. I could see why the people around her stopped asking questions. Nobody wants to feel stupid.

Her assessment results explained why. They showed two strong hidden drivers.

The first was going it alone. Somewhere in childhood, Laura’s brain had learned a rule: I can only count on myself. Needing anyone makes me weak.

The second was winning. Second place was not an option.

Put the two together, and her behavior makes sense. Being the smartest person in the room kept Laura in charge. If she always knew better, she never had to need anyone. And every conversation became a contest she could win.

As executive coach Marshall Goldsmith puts it, “Half the leaders I have met don’t need to learn what to do. They need to learn what to stop.”

Laura had built a life where she never had to need anyone. The cost was that no one could truly reach her: not her team, not even her best friend.

I see this pairing of drivers in high-performing leaders all the time. In many ways, it’s what got them to the top. But every driver has a shadow side.

People driven to go it alone tend to keep information to themselves, especially information that makes them look bad. People driven to win have trouble knowing a battle worth fighting from one that’s costing everyone around them.

I sat down with Laura and gently walked her through her results. I told her what her drivers were giving her and what they might cost her.

She listened. Then she said, “I’d like to take the test again.”

I told her the truth: It doesn’t work that way. A hidden driver isn’t a mood that changes depending on how you slept. It’s more like the foundation of a house. You can repaint the walls and rearrange the furniture, but the foundation stays where it was poured.

Here’s what I didn’t say out loud: Her request for a re-test was her drivers at work. To someone driven to go it alone, feedback sounds like “You need help.” To someone driven to win, a hard result feels like losing. So, she did what her drivers had always taught her to do. She tried to beat the test instead of learning from it.

That moment was a choice point: a small gap between what happened and what she did next. In that gap, Laura could have gotten curious. Instead, she reverted to the comfort of her drivers on autopilot.

A few years later, I heard that Laura had lost everything due to her own pride and arrogance: her company, her investors, her own money, and her reputation. I wasn’t surprised. Without awareness, there’s no way to change. Left unchecked, any of us can sabotage ourselves.

I’ve worked with other leaders who share Laura’s drivers and did change. They learned to reflect on themselves and take responsibility for their behavior. Laura never did.

Patterns begin in childhood. Attachment researchers have studied Laura’s pattern for decades. John Bowlby, the father of attachment theory, described people who become “compulsively self-reliant.” Adults with this pattern tend to hide or play down their feelings so they won’t look vulnerable, weak, or dependent on others.

Think of it like this: A child who learns that needing people isn’t safe builds a suit of armor. The armor protects the child. But decades later, the adult is still wearing it and wonders why no one can get close.

Fear makes everyone go quiet. Laura’s need to look smart came with a hidden price. Research on harsh bosses has found that abusive supervision makes employees afraid, and fear leads them to go silent. Harvard’s Amy Edmondson, who studies what she calls psychological safety, found that when it was missing, people were less willing to speak up, ask for help, or admit mistakes, so teams learned less.

Bad news stops traveling upward. Psychologists call this the “Mum Effect.” People tend to soften or hold back bad news, especially when it must go to someone powerful. Stanford professor Robert Sutton described a chilling example. After the 1986 Challenger disaster, physicist Richard Feynman found that NASA’s working engineers put the chance of losing a shuttle at roughly 1 in 100. NASA’s managers put it at 1 in 100,000. The truth had been softened at every step on its way up.

Now put the pieces together. Laura hid her own bad news about her failing company because her self-reliance wouldn’t let her look weak. Her team hid their bad news because she made them feel stupid for speaking up. She ended up leading from inside a bubble where nobody told her the truth, not even herself.

Her drivers weren’t what brought her down. Not seeing them was.

Let me be clear: Seeing someone’s hidden drivers doesn’t let them off the hook. Laura was responsible for how she treated people, and Elizabeth Holmes was convicted for what she did.

But labels like “bully,” “fraud,” or “villain” close the case. They let us feel safely different from the person we’re judging. Understanding drivers keeps the case open, and that makes change possible. You can’t change what you can’t see.

Seeing your hidden drivers isn’t a label or a verdict. It’s a mirror. And unlike Laura, you don’t need a re-test. You just need the willingness to look.

You Can See Everything promises full access. But none of us can see everything: not in a famous founder, not in the person across the table, and not in ourselves. Not without help and honesty.

All of us have a shadow side. Elizabeth Holmes’s story is an extreme one, but it’s a reminder of how much denial and ego can cost. Whether you’re in over your head at work or hiding the truth from people you care about, you're standing at a choice point. You can dig in deeper, or you can ask for help: from a therapist, a coach, or a trusted friend. Someone who can hold up a mirror and tell you what they see.

You can’t see everything. But you can learn to see yourself.

Bowlby, J. (1980). Attachment and Loss: Vol. 3. Loss: Sadness and Depression. Basic Books.

Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2), 350–383.

Feynman, R. P. (1986). Personal observations on the reliability of the Shuttle. Appendix F, Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident.

Goldsmith, M., & Reiter, M. (2007). What Got You Here Won't Get You There: How Successful People Become Even More Successful. Hyperion.

Kiewitz, C., Restubog, S. L. D., Shoss, M. K., Garcia, P. R. J. M., & Tang, R. L. (2016). Suffering in silence: Investigating the role of fear in the relationship between abusive supervision and defensive silence. Journal of Applied Psychology, 101(5), 731–742.

Mikulincer, M., & Shaver, P. R. (2016). Attachment in Adulthood: Structure, Dynamics, and Change (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

Sutton, R. I. (2010). The Mum Effect and filtering in organizations. Psychology Today.

#4888. BYD’s $10,000 EV blows a tire at nearly 90 mph — Watch what happens

BYD updated its lowest-priced electric car, the Seagull, which starts at around $10,000 in China, with a few extras, including a high-speed tire blowout system that stabilizes the vehicle at nearly 90 mph.

If the $10,000 price tag wasn’t enough, BYD is giving buyers even more reason to check out its entry-level electric hatch.

The Seagull is among BYD’s most popular vehicles, sold as the Dolphin Surf in Europe and the UK and as the Dolphin Mini in other global markets.

BYD launched the second-generation Seagull EV last week, starting at just 62,900 yuan, or about $9,500. That’s including BYD’s limited-time Super Trade-In incentive.

Regular prices start at 65,900 yuan ($9,900), which is still less than its predecessor. The first-generation Seagull EV started at 69,900 yuan ($10,500) without incentives, making it BYD’s most affordable purely electric vehicle in China.

For its second generation, the Seagull is bigger, more advanced, and adds a bit more luxury to the entry-level segment.

The new BYD Seagull is 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and has a 150 mm longer wheelbase than the previous model.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s electric hatch now offers room for five passengers, up from four seats that the first-gen Seagull had.

BYD added several new features with its latest tech, including a bigger 15.6″ infotainment screen with its DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a “140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system” as standard.

To showcase how the tire blowout system works, BYD put the updated electric hatch to the test at full speed.

BYD’s general manager of the Ocean Series, Zhang Zhuo, shared a video of the second-generation Seagull EV handling the blowout at 140 km/h, or about 87 mph, like it’s nothing.

The high-speed tire-blowout system lets the Seagull stay in its lane until it comes to a complete stop. Pretty impressive for an entry-level vehicle.

As you can see in the video, the new version also has an available roof-mounted LiDAR. Buyers can upgrade to the optional DiPilot 300 system with BYD’s God’s Eye intelligent driving assistance. The ADAS system provides features like City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

BYD added a few premium extras, including heating, ventilation, and a massage function to the front seats, plus ambient lighting, smart storage options, and a 50W wireless phone charger.

The new Seagull uses BYD’s Blade Batteries 2.0 and Flash Charging Technology. As such, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. A full recharge, or 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes 12 minutes to charge from 20% to 97%.

It’s available with two LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh, providing CLTC ranges of 320 km (199 miles) and 420 km (261 miles), respectively.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

The USA is now like a third world country when it comes to Electric Cars.

BYD is leaving the US so far behind in technology, it obviously it will never catch up as a result of it’s backwards MAGA leadership.

The second-gen Seagull also switches to front-wheel-drive (FWD) with a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) that its predecessor offered.

BYD’s new Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000), without a trade-in.

After launching the second-gen Seagull in China, BYD is expected to introduce the updated version overseas. It will likely be the second-generation Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.
